With new vehicle-entry restrictions set to take effect in Delhi from November 1, 2026, vehicle owners need to check whether their vehicles meet the prescribed emission standards before travelling to the national capital.
The seasonal restriction, which will remain in force until January 31, 2027, applies to non-Delhi-registered petrol and diesel vehicles that do not meet BS-VI emission standards. CNG and electric vehicles are exempt from this specific restriction.
The first step is to establish where your vehicle is registered.
The restriction applies differently depending on the vehicle's fuel type.
The most reliable way to identify your vehicle's Bharat Stage (BS) classification is through its official registration and manufacturer documents.
1. Check your Registration Certificate (RC). Look for fields such as ‘Fuel Norms’, ‘Emission Norms’ or ‘Norms Type’. The exact field name may vary across registration systems.
2. Check Form 22. Form 22 is the initial certificate of compliance issued by the vehicle manufacturer. It specifies the emission norms applicable to the vehicle. Do not confuse it with Form 21, which is the vehicle's sale certificate.
3. Check the Parivahan portal. If you do not have a physical copy of your RC, you can check your vehicle details through the government's Parivahan portal or the relevant state transport department's records.
4. Contact the manufacturer or an authorised dealer. If the emission classification is not available in your documents, share your Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) or chassis number with the manufacturer or an authorised dealer to obtain the vehicle's specifications.
The Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) can help identify your vehicle and retrieve its manufacturing details.

However, the VIN does not universally encode the Bharat Stage classification. Its characters and year codes vary across manufacturers. Therefore, do not rely on the manufacturing year or VIN alone to establish BS-VI compliance.
Once you have established your vehicle's registration location, fuel type and emission standard, use the following guide.
A valid PUC certificate does not automatically make a vehicle eligible to enter Delhi under the November 1 BS-VI restriction.
For instance, a non-Delhi-registered BS-IV petrol or diesel vehicle will remain restricted under this specific rule even if it has a valid PUC certificate. Similarly, a BS-VI-compliant vehicle must continue to meet applicable PUC requirements.
Meeting the BS-VI requirement does not automatically mean that a vehicle is permitted under every pollution-control measure.
GRAP restrictions are separate from the November 1 seasonal entry rule. Depending on the pollution-control stage in force, additional restrictions may apply to older petrol and diesel vehicles, goods vehicles and buses.
For instance, GRAP Stage 3 restrictions cover BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel or older light motor vehicles in
Delhi and specified NCR districts, subject to the operative order.
Owners should therefore check the latest GRAP restrictions and applicable government notifications before travelling.
Important: The November 1 restriction is scheduled to remain in force until January 31, 2027. The applicable rules may differ depending on vehicle category, registration location, fuel type and subsequent government directions. Meeting the specific BS-VI entry requirement does not guarantee exemption from other traffic or pollution-control restrictions.
Stuti Gupta is a Content Producer at Hindustan Times, based in New Delhi, where she is a part of the General News team, tasked with reporting on happenings across the country impacting domestic as well as international ecospheres. In her role at HT, she is responsible for keeping a track of incoming news updates, packaging stories and publishing them in a format best suited to their purpose. She holds a Bachelor’s in Mass Communication and Journalism from St Xavier’s, Mumbai and is partial towards working on international affairs. Apart from her interest in the geopolitical world, she is a keen reader, writer, orator, debater and learner who loves picking up new information. She has been recognized for her previous literary work at the international level with a Gold Finalist, Gold and Silver Award in various participating years at the Queen’s Commonwealth Essay Competition along with winning the third prize and getting her story published in Children’s World in 2017. Barring academic and professional pursuits, she has a passion for travelling to new places, exploring new cultures and cuisines, documenting them through words and pictures and interacting with people from diverse backgrounds.
